case_study_insert.main_stem: Coppergate Precision Castings (CPC) is a private limited company in the metal manufacturing sector, producing aluminium brake discs and calipers for passenger cars and light commercial vehicles, with a workforce of 80. Founded in 2004 by Denise Marlow, CPC operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership and supplies three national vehicle assemblers. CPC plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new automated casting and CNC machining cell, financed by a $750,000 ten-year bank loan and $450,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $384,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.50 a unit and a selling price of $22.50, and produces 120,000 units a year. CPC faces rising defect rates on the machining line and absenteeism of 6% on night shifts.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The casting cell poured 30,000 discs last quarter at a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.2% a year ago, while scrap metal waste fell from 8.5% to 6.1% of output. Customer complaints from assemblers fell from 44 to 27 per month. Average machining set-up time improved to 2.4 hours. A market survey of 480 fleet procurement managers found that 58% would specify lighter aluminium castings and 49% rate local supply above price. Night-shift absenteeism stands at 6%, and 16 of 80 machinists have not completed training on the new CNC controls; off-the-job training at the technical college costs $1,150 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Coppergate Precision Castings as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.85 to $13.60 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Wholesale aluminium ingot prices have risen 15.2% year-on-year and manufacturing input-cost inflation is running at 7.4%, while national consumer spending on new vehicles grew 2.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: CPC plans to finance part of its new casting cell with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CPC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit is an internal source with no interest or repayment, so CPC keeps full control of the $1,200,000 casting and CNC cell without committing to fixed debt service on top of the $384,000 fixed costs it already carries each year. This is especially valuable while aluminium input costs are inflating 15.2%, because every dollar saved on interest can absorb raw-material volatility without raising the $22.50 selling price above what fleet assemblers will accept.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids placing the new line at risk. A $750,000 ten-year bank loan would typically be secured against CPC's assets, and if national vehicle demand slowed, the lender could recall the loan or force a restructuring that jeopardises the 120,000-unit programme. Retained profit also preserves Denise Marlow's ownership and decision-making authority within CPC's autocratic structure, with no external lender imposing covenants on how the casting cell is run or when a second expansion phase is financed. It keeps CPC self-sufficient and protects its assembler contracts from disruption.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Coppergate Precision Castings and its casting-cell expansion.

questions.question_text: CPC is launching its new lightweight aluminium brake-disc range for fleet buyers. Consider exhibiting at the National Automotive Components Expo, advertising in a specialist casting trade journal, or running a targeted social media campaign on LinkedIn. Which should CPC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National Automotive Components Expo: Exhibiting gives CPC face-to-face access to the procurement managers of the three national vehicle assemblers it already supplies, plus new fleet accounts; live demonstrations of the lighter castings can close orders on the spot and build trust that print never achieves. However, stand space, transport and staffing for a four-day expo would absorb a sizeable slice of the $1,200,000 expansion budget, results depend on one week a year, and pulling CPC's autocratic, engineering-led managers off the floor risks worsening the 6% night-shift absenteeism during the ramp-up.

Trade journal advertising: Quarter-page adverts in a specialist casting journal, a few thousand dollars per issue, reach technical buyers, suit the long sales cycles of assembler contracts and build credibility for CPC's 2.6% defect rate story. Drawbacks are slow lead times, no guarantee of enquiries, and a readership that skews to foundry engineers rather than the fleet procurement managers who specify CPC's most valuable contracts.

Targeted social media campaign: Promoted LinkedIn content aimed at procurement and engineering managers segmented by vehicle-assembly plants costs a fraction of the expo, is measurable through click-through and enquiry forms, and can showcase the weight-saving and local-supply advantages that 58% and 49% of surveyed fleet managers respectively value. It requires consistent content and sales follow-up, but it is the only option whose reach matches CPC's national assembler ambitions cost-effectively.

Recommendation: CPC should choose the targeted social media campaign. It is cheapest, measurable, and precisely targets the segment identified in its own market research while the $1,200,000 cell beds in. The expo is rejected as too expensive and too occasional for a single-plant caster funding a bank-loan-financed expansion; trade journal advertising is rejected as too passive and too narrow to win new assembler contracts quickly. CPC can revisit the expo in 2027 once the cell is proven and order coverage exceeds 30,000 units a quarter.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CPC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CPC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the expo and trade journal advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: CPC runs a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership and night-shift absenteeism of 6%. Explain two benefits for CPC of autocratic leadership in its new casting cell.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Under autocratic leadership, Denise Marlow can issue clear, non-negotiable instructions on CNC machining tolerances, safety interlocks and night-shift priorities, which suits precision casting work where a single error scraps a disc and wastes aluminium at 15.2% above last year's cost. Fast, top-down decisions mean the new cell reaches full output quickly after the $1,200,000 investment, without time lost to committee debate, and the chain of command stays short and unambiguous for 80 employees.

Point 2: Autocratic leadership strengthens accountability for quality. When the 2.6% defect rate or 6.1% scrap waste drifts upward, managers can reassign work, enforce inspection sign-off and correct poor practice immediately — something a laissez-faire style could not deliver while the 16 untrained machinists learn the new controls. Clear, consistent expectations also reassure the night shift, where absenteeism already stands at 6%, because everyone knows the standard required and the consequences of missing it, although CPC must still fund the $1,150 per-employee off-the-job training so staff can actually meet those standards.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CPC's absenteeism, defect rate and expansion.

questions.question_text: CPC must fill two CNC supervisor vacancies in the new casting cell. Consider promoting two proven machinists from the night shift, or recruiting qualified CNC supervisors externally. Which should CPC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal promotion from the night shift: Promoting two machinists to supervisor rewards loyalty, directly tackles the 6% night-shift absenteeism, costs nothing in agency fees, keeps casting knowledge inside CPC, and signals to all 80 employees that hard work is rewarded — a powerful motivator under autocratic leadership. Limitations: the two promoted machinists still need CNC certification, CPC loses two good operators, and newly promoted staff may lack the confidence to enforce autocratic discipline fairly on former peers.

External recruitment of qualified CNC supervisors: Advertising and agency fees for two experienced supervisors would run to thousands of dollars, but they arrive certified, bring fresh best practice from comparable casting cells, and need no training time on the $1,200,000 line, protecting the 120,000-unit programme from day one. Drawbacks: higher salary demands, integration risk with current staff, 4-10 week notice periods before they start, and no motivational signal to the night shift, whose absenteeism could persist or worsen.

Decision: CPC should choose internal promotion, supported by the $1,150 off-the-job college course for both supervisors and the remaining 16 untrained machinists. Internal recruitment is cheaper, faster to mobilise while the cell ramps up, and directly addresses night-shift absenteeism and morale under an autocratic regime. External recruitment is rejected because certified CNC supervisors command salary premiums that strain the $750,000 loan-funded budget before the cell generates cash, and outside hires cannot match internal knowledge of CPC's three assembler tolerance requirements. If the cell fails two consecutive quality audits, CPC should reconsider one external specialist hire.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment approaches with limited application to CPC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the advantages and drawbacks of internal and external recruitment in the context of CPC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of CPC with a well-justified decision covering cost, speed, capability and motivation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CPC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $384,000 ÷ ($22.50 − $14.50) = $384,000 ÷ $8.00 = 48,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 48,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $22.50 − $14.50 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CPC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 48,000-unit break-even output with the current 120,000-unit production to confirm the disc line is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 72,000 units, before committing to ramp the new cell to full capacity.
2. A contribution per unit of $8.00 lets CPC model assembler price negotiations, for example a 5% discount to $21.38 a unit would cut contribution to $6.88, showing managers exactly how much extra volume would be needed to keep covering the $384,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing the $384,000 fixed costs and the $8.00 contribution helps managers test whether the 120,000-unit programme can service the $750,000 bank loan and the $450,000 retained profit before the next capital request, and whether to delay phase two of the expansion.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost ($384,000 ÷ 120,000 units + $14.50 = $17.70 a unit, i.e. average total cost of $17.70) against the $22.50 selling price to track the $4.80 profit margin, target the 6.1% scrap-metal waste and 2.6% defect rate for reduction, and renegotiate the $14.50 variable cost with aluminium suppliers amid the 15.2% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 48,000 units ($384,000 ÷ $8.00) | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 ($22.50 − $14.50) | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 72,000 units against 120,000-unit output; 5% discount modelling to $21.38 (contribution $6.88) against $384,000 fixed costs; feasibility check for servicing the $750,000 ten-year bank loan within the $1,200,000 casting-cell programme funded with $450,000 retained profit; unit-cost benchmarking at $17.70 (vs $22.50 price and $14.50 variable cost) to attack the 6.1% scrap-metal waste, the 2.6% defect rate and the 15.2% aluminium inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CPC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CPC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.71 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.18 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $260,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $525,000; 2025 current assets = $175,000 + $305,000 + $85,000 = $565,000. 2024: $525,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.50; 2025: $565,000 ÷ $330,000 = 1.71. For the stricter measure, 2024: ($525,000 − $210,000) ÷ $350,000 = $315,000 ÷ $350,000 = 0.90; 2025: ($565,000 − $175,000) ÷ $330,000 = $390,000 ÷ $330,000 = 1.18.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. The improvement is not inventory-led: inventories actually fell from $210,000 to $175,000 as the casting cell's throughput and the 2.6% defect rate improved, while current liabilities fell from $350,000 to $330,000. Cash rose from $55,000 to $85,000, giving CPC headroom to service the $750,000 bank loan while funding the $1,200,000 expansion. The acid test moving from 0.90 to 1.18 means CPC can cover short-term debts without selling castings, a genuine quality improvement in the balance sheet. However, trade receivables climbed from $260,000 to $305,000 — if any of the three national vehicle assemblers pays late, the stronger 2025 position could deteriorate quickly, and floor stock of finished discs must remain sufficient to honour contract schedules.

Conclusion: CPC's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures strengthened (1.50 to 1.71 overall; 0.90 to 1.18 excluding stock), the improvement is genuine rather than inventory-driven, and current liabilities are falling. CPC should tighten credit control on assembler invoices, maintain the inventory discipline that delivered the 2.6% defect rate, and only commit to phase two of the expansion once receivables growth is contained.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether CPC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CPC of introducing computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) and robotics in its new casting cell.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: CAM and robotic handling give CPC consistent, micrometre-level control of casting and machining, driving the 2.6% defect rate toward the 4.2%-to-2.6% trajectory trend and slashing the 6.1% scrap-metal waste. Fewer rejected discs protect the $22.50 selling price, reassure the three national vehicle assemblers, and let the 80 employees concentrate on quality supervision and exception handling rather than repetitive fettling — easing the night-shift absenteeism pressure because overtime and weekend cover fall.

Disadvantage: The $1,200,000 capital cost plus integration, maintenance contracts and programming adds a heavy fixed-cost burden on top of the $384,000 a year CPC already carries, raising the output needed to stay ahead of break-even. Robots also reduce demand for unskilled casting-floor labour, creating a risk of redundancies or morale damage within an autocratic culture, and a single programming fault can halt the whole cell, so CPC must complete CNC certification for all 80 staff and retain skilled manual oversight before full switch-on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CPC's defect rate, costs, training and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 15.2% rise in aluminium input costs will affect CPC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise to 5.00%: The $750,000 ten-year bank loan, if variable-rate, would cost about $5,600 extra interest a year (0.75% of the outstanding balance); any working-capital facilities and any future borrowing for the $1,200,000 cell also become pricier. The cash impact is real but modest, and assemblers' procurement budgets may tighten slightly, though the 2.8% growth in national vehicle spending is a partial offset. CPC could mitigate by negotiating a fixed rate.

Minimum wage increase of 5.8% to $13.60: With 80 production and packing staff, the wage bill rises by roughly 5.8%. If average earnings are near $13.60 an hour for 2,080 hours, each worker adds about $1,550 a year, or around $124,000 across the workforce — material against $384,000 of fixed costs, though productivity gains from the new cell (120,000 units from 80 staff = 1,500 units per worker) can absorb part of it through lower overtime and reduced absenteeism.

Aluminium input cost inflation of 15.2%: CPC's $14.50 variable cost is dominated by aluminium ingot; a 15.2% rise on the metal component (roughly $9-$10 per unit) adds about $1.40-$1.50 per disc. Across 120,000 units that is roughly $168,000-$180,000 a year, compressing contribution per unit from $8.00 toward $6.50-$6.60, cutting margin of safety, and directly eroding the return that justifies the $1,200,000 expansion.

Conclusion: The 15.2% aluminium input-cost inflation will have the greatest impact. It strikes every unit CPC produces (120,000 a year), compounds against the 7.4% wider input-cost inflation, and outweighs the wage rise (~$124,000) and the interest-rate rise (~$5,600); it is also the hardest to pass on, because CPC's three assembler contracts fix pricing annually. CPC must hedge aluminium purchases, renegotiate assembler alloy surcharges, and pursue scrap reduction below 6.1% before signing phase two of the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CPC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CPC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CPC with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
